content: Data collected by community health workers (CHWs) should be integrated into the national health information system. A structured process must be established to utilize this data effectively for revising the national health plan, adapting advocacy and communication strategies, mobilizing resources, and engaging with relevant actors in water, sanitation, hygiene (WASH), and clean air initiatives. The national pneumonia and diarrhea plan should include locally relevant goals and measurable targets, along with indicators to assess progress and strategies to ensure the availability of necessary data. Epidemiological and programmatic data are typically gathered through national health information systems and periodic surveys, such as the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS). Additional data sources, like the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response system in Africa, provide valuable insights. The World Health Organization (WHO) compiles, updates, and reports annually on household energy use, while the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) publishes biennial reports on access to water and sanitation, with detailed analyses based on location and socioeconomic status. Opportunities exist to link data collection efforts with broader initiatives, such as the United Nations Commission on Information and Accountability (CoIA). Countries are accountable to their populations and the global community for reducing the burden of pneumonia and diarrhea. Accountability ensures recognition of the problem and fulfillment of commitments by all stakeholders. It demonstrates how actions and investments lead to tangible results and improved long-term outcomes, identifying successes, areas for improvement, and priorities requiring attention. Accountability frameworks define methodologies and data sources for indicators, assign responsibilities to stakeholders, and outline processes for monitoring and evaluating progress. For example, the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) provides a foundation for developing accountability frameworks at national, regional, and global levels. Civil society groups, community organizations, and faith-based entities play a critical role in supporting citizens and holding governments accountable. Families and communities contribute to local-level accountability, and mechanisms to empower these groups should be established or strengthened. At the global level, initiatives like Countdown to 2015 monitor intervention coverage as a proxy for mortality reduction. The United Nations CoIA has emphasized the importance of large-scale population-based surveys to complement national health information systems. Collaboration with other programs and sectors is essential for pneumonia and diarrhea control. For instance, nutrition programs promote breastfeeding, hygiene programs prevent diarrhea, and cholera task forces implement prevention and response measures. National working groups should engage with these programs and include representatives from non-health sectors, such as education, environment, and public transportation, to enhance coordination and collaboration. Examples of integration include supply chain optimization, clean energy access, and household water and air quality interventions. Parallel supply systems for health commodities often result in inefficiencies, such as fragmented management, storage issues, and stock-outs. Integrated supply chains, as seen in Senegal, Tunisia, and Vietnam, aim to address these challenges. Senegal employs a fully integrated supply chain with a moving warehouse model, while Tunisia uses segmented integration for temperature-sensitive products. These approaches optimize transportation and delivery routes, improving efficiency and reducing waste. Energy poverty, which affects billions of people, has significant implications for health, economic development, and climate change. The United Nations' Sustainable Energy for All (SEFA) initiative, launched in 2012, aims to achieve universal access to electricity and modern household energy systems by 2030. Programs like the United Nations Foundation's Alliance for Clean Cookstoves promote clean and safe household energy solutions. WHO's household energy database and indoor air quality guidelines provide critical data and recommendations for reducing harmful emissions and associated diseases. In Rwanda, WHO collaborates with the government and stakeholders to address reliance on solid fuels for cooking and heating, which contributes to indoor air pollution and deforestation. The DelAgua Health Rwanda program distributes water filters and efficient cookstoves to vulnerable households, targeting the poorest 30% of the population. These technologies reduce fuel use and indoor air pollution without requiring electricity. Plans are underway to evaluate the health impacts of these interventions. Private sector involvement is crucial for health interventions, particularly in areas like technology development, clean energy supply, and financing. Associations of healthcare professionals, manufacturers, and community groups should be included in planning and implementing pneumonia and diarrhea actions to achieve broader population coverage. United Nations agencies and donors provide technical support, guidelines, and tools for situation analysis and action plan development, as well as monitoring progress. Innovations can eliminate barriers to health and improve outcomes. Mobile phone technology enables rapid dissemination of information and real-time health data reporting. E-learning tools expand training options for health workers at lower costs. New vaccines and delivery devices can be integrated into immunization programs, while task-shifting increases capacity for delivering key interventions. Innovative approaches to inter-sectoral collaboration should be incorporated into planning and evaluation processes. For example, the United Nations Commission on Life-Saving Commodities for Women and Children focuses on supply and delivery innovations to expand access to essential health services. In Malawi, mobile technology has been used to improve the supply of child health medicines for community case management (CCM). Health Surveillance Assistants (HSAs), who provide CCM services, often face challenges in maintaining medicine supplies due to poor infrastructure. The cStock system, a web-based SMS platform, was developed to monitor and manage community-level medicine stocks, ensuring timely resupply and reducing stock-outs.
